name: Polyglutamic acid
lead: Polyglutamic acid (PGA) is a polymer of the amino acid glutamic acid, existing as gamma-PGA (linked through the side-chain carboxyl) and alpha-PGA (linked through the alpha-carboxyl). Both forms are water-soluble, amphiphilic and negatively charged.[1]

In skincare, gamma-PGA is used as a water-binding ingredient. Brands that include it in serums and moisturizers position it as a humectant that draws and holds water at the skin surface for a smoother, plumper, more hydrated look, often alongside hyaluronic acid.[1][2] Grokipedia states that it absorbs many times its weight in water and holds more than hyaluronic acid; this comes from an AI-generated source and is not tied to a cited comparative trial.[2]

Gamma-PGA is produced by Bacillus species through fermentation and is a major constituent of the Japanese food natto.[1] The best-documented human trials involve alpha-PGA as a carrier in the chemotherapy conjugate paclitaxel poliglumex, and oral gamma-PGA has been tested in a few small trials for blood sugar, lipids and cervical lesions. No trials found test PGA for skin appearance.[3][8][9][10][11][12]

paras: Gamma-PGA is typically made of mixed D and L glutamate, while alpha-PGA is mostly L-form. Gamma-PGA is described as non-immunogenic and biodegradable.[1] Industrial gamma-PGA comes from bacterial fermentation involving glutamate racemase and a polymer synthesis operon, and alpha-PGA is made by chemical ring-opening polymerisation.[1] Gamma-PGA also forms part of the Bacillus anthracis capsule.[1]

Gamma-PGA is listed as a cosmeceutical ingredient.[1] Grokipedia describes it as a humectant that improves skin barrier function and reduces signs of ageing, with water absorption up to 5000 times its weight, claims that are unverified.[2]
Alpha-PGA serves as a delivery aid in paclitaxel poliglumex.[1] Gamma-PGA research includes drug, insulin and vaccine-antigen delivery, and a possible food thickener role.[1][4]

In skincare, polyglutamic acid is sold as a humectant meant to leave the skin surface more hydrated, so that it looks plumper and less dull. Products usually pair it with hyaluronic acid, glycerin or ceramides in serums and moisturizers, and brands describe it as a larger-molecule water binder that sits on the skin surface.[1][2] Grokipedia states that it absorbs many times its weight in water and holds more than hyaluronic acid, a comparison that comes from an AI-generated source and is not tied to a cited head-to-head trial.[2]

The mechanism offered is physical: the long polymer chain carries many negative charges and is water-soluble and amphiphilic, so it can bind water and metal ions, which Wikipedia describes as the basis of its role in cosmeceuticals.[1] The cosmetic-ingredient literature cited for it is largely about production and material properties; reviews concentrate on microbial biosynthesis and on drug-delivery and food uses rather than on skin-appearance trials.[4][13][14]

Gamma-PGA has long been known as the sticky, stringy component of natto, the Japanese fermented soybean food made with Bacillus subtilis, and as the capsule material of Bacillus anthracis, where it helps the bacterium evade the immune system.[1] Goto and Kunioka studied its biosynthesis and hydrolysis from a B. subtilis strain in 1992.[1] The medical side advanced when a 1998 Cancer Research paper by Li and colleagues reported complete regression of established tumours in animals with a PGA-paclitaxel conjugate, the basis of the later paclitaxel poliglumex trials.[1][3][8] Wikipedia lists the cosmeceutical role and notes that medical use of gamma-PGA itself is largely pre-clinical, including work on wound healing and microneedle delivery of insulin.[1]

Gamma-PGA is an important part of the Bacillus anthracis capsule, where it is described as hiding the bacterium from the immune system.[1] In natto it is made by Bacillus subtilis during fermentation of soybeans.[1] Industrial production relies on fermentation, and reviews focus on strains that do not need costly glutamic acid feeding, on metabolic engineering of Bacillus and on cheaper feedstocks.[13][14]

Eating natto can lead to delayed anaphylaxis in some people, and a 2025 review of novel foods in the journal Dermatologie lists it among foods with allergenic potential.[15] That concerns the whole fermented food rather than purified PGA.

Gamma-PGA based flocculants have been used in water treatment, including for refugee water supplies via the International Organization for Migration, and PGA bound to membranes has shown high heavy-metal sorption in laboratory work.[1] Polyglutamic acid segments also occur in natural proteins such as bone sialoprotein, where they help bind hydroxyapatite.[16] Wikipedia also cites a study in which PGA removed 99.8 percent of lead ions from water by low-pressure ultrafiltration.[1]
No studies found testing polyglutamic acid for appearance, skin or hair. Human trials of other uses exist.

Paclitaxel poliglumex, which links paclitaxel to polyglutamic acid to reduce peak exposure to free drug, was compared with standard therapy in advanced non-small cell lung cancer. A phase III trial in performance-status 2 patients combined it with carboplatin versus paclitaxel plus carboplatin,[3] and a phase III trial of 849 previously treated patients compared it with docetaxel, with median survival of 6.9 months in both arms.[8] Registered ovarian cancer trials include a phase III study of 1,157 participants and a 32-person phase I study.[5][6]

Oral gamma-PGA was given in a randomized double-blind phase II trial in women with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia 1, with 1,500 mg for 4 weeks versus placebo and histologic regression at 12 weeks as the primary endpoint.[9] Natto rich in gamma-PGA was examined in randomized crossover studies for its effect on blood glucose in the early phase after meals,[10][11] and a randomized trial of high-molecular-weight gamma-PGA examined lipid metabolism in rats and humans.[12]

One registered study evaluated an anti-redness dermocosmetic and intense pulsed light for rosacea (n=60); it tested a product rather than PGA specifically.[7] Reviews describe microbial PGA biosynthesis and its biopharmaceutical, biomedical and food applications.[4][13]

card.summary: A bacterial-fermentation humectant polymer marketed in skincare; real clinical use is as a drug carrier, not for appearance.
card.note: Superior-to-hyaluronic-acid claims come from AI-generated or marketing sources, not from cited trials.

quick.overview:
Polyglutamic acid is a long chain of glutamic acid produced by Bacillus bacteria, also found in natto. Skincare brands use it as a water-holding ingredient.
Human trials involve cancer-drug conjugates rather than skin; none were found testing it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: The polymer is water-soluble and carries many negative charges, which lets it bind water and metals. In medicine it is attached to drugs such as paclitaxel to change how they are delivered.
quick.risks: Gamma-PGA is described as biodegradable and non-immunogenic. Wikipedia notes its medical use is largely pre-clinical, and safety data for topical cosmetic use are lacking.

chain: Gamma-PGA is applied in a serum or moisturizer
Its charged polymer chains bind water at the skin surface
Skin looks and feels more hydrated and smoother
angle.text: Skincare products list polyglutamic acid as a humectant to boost surface hydration, so skin looks plumper and less dull. This is the way it is marketed and discussed; trials of PGA on skin appearance have not been found.
